body_markdown:
“Early adopter” is a marketing term for someone who buys a product or service before the general public is keen to the notion. Their risk tolerance is high, and they revel in getting in on the ground floor. Being an early adopter of Slate Automotive’s EV truck means bragging about your build date and buying it without a test drive. But the lucky ones who live near one of Slate’s events get to hop inside an unfinished prototype for a quick ride. It’s nothing like the traditional way of automotive retailing, and that’s why I drove over 250 miles to check one out in the flesh.


Like many automotive journalists, I vocally support this little truck and the company behind it. Even better, I’m putting my money where my mouth is, as my Slate is slated for delivery in the first quarter of 2027. That’s a big jump for me, as I don’t consider myself an early adopter who makes large purchases without hands-on research. (For all the marketing nerds out there, consider me a “laggard.”)


Hagerty Media


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


My five-hour journey was uneventful, but I was disappointed upon arrival. Slate’s event in Plano, TX was more of a[marketing activation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marketing_activation) , and it lived in the parking garage of one of those “live, work, play” mixed-use developments populating our nation. Rain from the remnants of Hurricane Polo crammed everything inside said parking structure, but it stopped long enough to ensure I wouldn’t hear raindrops that would test the body’s NVH engineering.


Even worse, the rain didn’t stop long enough to dry out the roads. I was hoping to cajole the Slate representative to floor it from a standstill to see if the little EV truck would give me a tire chirp or two, but the slickness present meant traction control would hamper any attempted fun. These were the worst conditions to experience a new vehicle, not to mention I wasn’t even driving the darn thing.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


I hopped into a Slate prototype with a yellow wrap; its undercarriage was still dripping from the last ride with an intender. The door handle appears to be metal, and the plastic-clad portals close with the reassuring thud of a vintage sedan. The interior is sparse, more so in this prototype, with shiny, featureless plastic textures that look like a rough draft of an essay. The rotary HVAC control knobs are a delightful throwback, though I wish they had more heft and resistance like the dials in my Ranger.


Since I wasn’t driving, I had plenty of time to analyze the platform’s[design volumes](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/vellum-venom/vellum-venom-a-glossary-of-automotive-design-terms/#:~:text=Volumes%3A%20The%20basic%20shape%20of%20a%20vehicle%2C%20the%C2%A0outline%20of%20the%20body%20work%20when%20seen%20from%20the%20side.%20More%20info%20here.) . The Slate is significantly different from yesteryear’s compact truck. While old-school compacts prioritize the cargo hold over the cabin, the Slate feels like it gives passenger and cargo space equal treatment. The five-foot bed looks even smaller thanks to massive bed rails, and there’s a large dashboard that pushes you far behind the action. You’d be in the bed of an OG compact if it sported a dash this foreboding, but the thicker dash makes for a voluminous footwell and a more car-like seating position. The Slate’s roof is also modern-SUV spacious, with room for big hats and side-curtain airbags. (I reckon this[mandatory safety feature](https://www.nbcnews.com/id/wbna20604563#:~:text=The%20National%20Highway%20Traffic%20Safety%20Administration%20on%20Wednesday%20issued%20new%20rules%20requiring%20the%20improved%20safety%20protections%20in%20new%20passenger%20vehicles%20by%20September%202012.) put the final nail in the original Ranger’s coffin.)


Pleasantries were exchanged between the Slate rep behind the wheel and yours truly, and she activated the truck with a flick of its column-mounted shifter. As we left the parking garage, I noticed my bucket seat was far more supportive than the throne in my Ranger. It was library-silent at low speeds, as we’d expect from an EV at low throttle inputs. I turned the window cranks (a feature Slate promotes on social media) and noted it took way more rotations than the handles in my vintage Mercury sedans. While I wouldn’t mind adding power windows in the future, the standard power locks did their job with a reassurance worthy of the truck’s substantial exterior door handles.


Once we drove out of the shopping plaza, I asked the rep for a favor: give some space to traffic in front of you and floor it from a standstill. She was comfortable with my ask, though she could only drive on the wet roads around the plaza. I wasn’t surprised when the Slate’s throttle mapping felt sluggish, as speed only built up after the speedometer hit 3 or 4 mph. The electric motor barely eked out the spaceship noises commonly heard in Teslas and Rivians. The regenerative brakes on its one-pedal driving configuration, however, felt spot on: Slate Automotive seemingly cares to give you maximum regeneration, and lets you modulate the throttle to your own tastes.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


I worked the two shiny plastic gloveboxes on the prototype’s dashboard; their actions were a bit fussy, and the storage space was not as deep as I hoped. Perhaps width makes up for depth, and the two USB-C charging ports are conveniently located for smartphone and audio integration.


The prototype didn’t have Slate’s famous “use your phone, we ain’t giving you a touchscreen!” docking station, nor was an audio system present. That’s unfortunate, as I was hoping to see all the goodies influencers and journalists experienced when Slate opened a marketing activation in Los Angeles. (This[YouTube video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qBJia4xhgec) made it look amazing.) Maybe the return policy on Slate’s accessories is generous. Or maybe I won’t even bother buying them. Time will tell.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


I took a long, hard look at both Slate prototypes before I left the parking garage, noticing how the massive B-pillar is probably needed to safely convert the truck into an (optional) SUV body. I was tempted to whip out my phone, ask to pop open the frunk, and pepper the staff with more questions like a social media influencer seeking content. But my memories of working trade shows as a teenager are strong, reminding me to shut my trap and enjoy my early adoption status.


Instead, I noted the removable panel in the bed’s floor, as it looked perfect for storing valuable tools away from prying eyes. But it’s only removed for customers upgrading their Slate to that SUV body style. The modularity is impressive, and it reminds me of the Chevrolet El Camino. Both vehicles leverage a multi-purpose platform to be all things to all people. The all-new Slate is clearly safer, quieter, faster, and more comfortable than a truck. It feels like a car, an appeal it shares with El Caminos that lived in an S-10 world.


As I pondered the El Camino-ization of the electric vehicle, I used my phone to capture a moment that stuck with me. Vinyl graphics on both trucks aside, the Slate’s bolt-on angular body makes the tapered, contoured, and finessed steel stampings of Ford’s Ranger look like the curvaceous 1962 Ferrari GTO. That analogy could be the textbook definition of “clutching at straws,” but my internal monologue was interrupted by a fellow attendee who had walked over to check out my truck.


Turns out he also owns a Ranger, but with the less bulletproof 4.0-liter Cologne V-6. The Slate was his alternative to spending $5000 on timing chain/engine maintenance on a motor with 180,000 miles. He indirectly asked for my thoughts on his conundrum, and I openly admitted we had two different use cases for the same truck. I mentioned the whole early adopter thing, which landed pancake-flat with him.


We parted ways with a smile, and as I drove home I pondered this notion:


> “A new Slate will be close to $28,000 out the door in Texas, and that figure is a heckuva lot higher than $5000. You only *need* this truck if you don’t already have a good Ranger, but I still want it.”
